What does the Maricopa County Recorder do?

The Maricopa County Recorder's Office keeps the public record of documents that affect land in the county, and it also runs voter registration and mail voting. The office reports more than 52 million recorded documents and voter registration for more than 2.6 million eligible voters. For a home seller the relevant work is recording the deed that moves title and the deed of trust that releases or replaces the old loan.

The office cannot give legal advice, will not help complete documents, and does not provide notary services. If you are unsure which form to record, a title company, estate planner or attorney has to answer that. The recording phone line is 602-506-3535.

Maricopa County is the largest county in Arizona. It covers 9,224 square miles, had 4,420,568 residents in the 2020 census, and contains fifteen cities and ten towns, from Phoenix (the county seat) to Gila Bend and Wickenburg. Recording happens at one downtown office no matter where in that area the house sits.

Where and how can you record a deed in Maricopa County?

You can record in person, by mail or electronically. The document has to be an original or a government-issued certified copy. The downtown office is at 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200, Phoenix, AZ 85003, open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., excluding holidays, with no appointment needed. An in-person original comes back to you right away.

  • In person: cash, card or check are accepted. Check payee is Maricopa County Recorder.
  • By mail: send to Attn. Copy Desk at the same address with a check, cashier's check or money order. The recorded original is mailed back to the return address in 2 to 4 weeks, and the office does not promise same-day recording of mailed documents.
  • Electronic: digital recording accounts are built for high-volume customers. A single document can go through a third-party submitter instead.

Most sellers never visit. The title or escrow company at closing records the deed for you, so the practical task is making sure the deed and its affidavit are signed correctly before closing day.

How much does it cost to record a document in Maricopa County?

The standard fee is $30 per document, regardless of length, under A.R.S. 11-475. The Recorder's published fee page lists the rest.

Source: Maricopa County Recorder fee schedule.

The office collects fees up front, so a mailed deed should arrive with the right total. Ask your title company which separate charges, if any, appear on your settlement statement.

What must a Maricopa County deed include to be recorded?

A deed needs either an Affidavit of Property Value or an exemption code. The Recorder's FAQ says the affidavit records the selling price, date of sale and other details about the sale, and a deed that fits an exemption can carry the code on its face instead. The office cannot say which code fits your deed.

The statute behind this is A.R.S. 11-1133. A deed that transfers title, and any contract of sale, must have an affidavit signed by seller and buyer or their agents, on a form approved by the Department of Revenue. It asks for these items:

  • Names, mailing addresses and phone numbers of buyer and seller
  • The name and address for the tax statement
  • The complete legal description, the situs address and the assessor's parcel number
  • The date of sale and total consideration, including cash down payment and the type of financing
  • Whether personal property received is 5% or more of the price
  • The relationship of the parties, and for a house, whether it will be owner-occupied or rented

The recorder must refuse a deed that lacks a complete affidavit unless it carries an exemption notation. Form rules for the document itself, such as a caption and margins, come from A.R.S. 11-480 and the office's form requirements page.

How does recording connect to property tax in Maricopa County?

The deed you record is how the Assessor learns who the new owner is and where to send the tax statement, which is why the affidavit asks for a tax-statement address. The Treasurer then bills that owner. If a house sells in the fall, find out whether the first half has been paid. In Maricopa County it is due October 1 and delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 (November 2 in 2026, since the first fell on a Sunday), and the full-year deadline is December 31.

Property tax is a lien, and A.R.S. 42-17153 says it attaches on January 1 of the tax year and ranks ahead of other liens except state liens and tax liens from other years. A title company will therefore expect any unpaid tax to be settled from your proceeds at closing. The Maricopa County Treasurer takes questions on amounts due at 602-506-8511.

The Assessor's site also links to Maricopa Title Alert, a free document registration notification service provided through the Recorder's Office. Owners who inherited a house or live out of state can use it to keep an eye on their title. The Treasurer collects for more than 1,800 tax districts, including cities, schools, community colleges and special districts, so one bill covers many levies. The Treasurer's site also lists excess proceeds from foreclosure sales that brought in more than the amount owed, under A.R.S. 33-812.

What should a seller check before recording day?

A short checklist prevents most rejected recordings.

  • Names on the deed match the names on the title exactly, including any trust.
  • The legal description and parcel number match the prior deed.
  • The Affidavit of Property Value is signed, or an exemption code is written on the deed.
  • The document is an original, signed, and any notary block is complete.
  • The return address is typed on the upper left of the first page.
  • The fee total is correct for the number of documents, at $30 each.

Where a house passes through a probate or trust, the deed chain can be longer than usual, and each document recorded carries its own fee. Ask the title company for a list of what will be recorded and a total.

It charges $30 per document for most documents, regardless of page count, under A.R.S. 11-475. Plats and surveys cost $24 for the first page and $20 for each added page. Copies are $1 per page and certification is $3 per document.

Where is the Maricopa County Recorder's office?

The downtown office is at 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200, Phoenix, AZ 85003. It is open Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., excluding holidays, and no appointment is needed to record in person.

Can I mail a deed to the Maricopa County Recorder?

Yes. Mail the original, with the right fee by check, cashier's check or money order, to Attn. Copy Desk at 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200, Phoenix, AZ 85003. The recorded document is mailed back in 2 to 4 weeks, and the office does not guarantee recording on the day it receives a mailed document.

Does a deed need an Affidavit of Property Value in Maricopa County?

Yes, unless it carries an exemption code. A.R.S. 11-1133 requires the affidavit on a deed that transfers title, and the recorder must refuse a deed without a complete affidavit or an exemption notation. The Recorder's office cannot advise which exemption applies.

Will the Maricopa County Recorder help me fill out a deed?

No. The office cannot provide legal advice or help complete documents, and it does not offer notary services. Use a title company, estate planner or attorney. For recording questions, call 602-506-3535.

Where do you record a deed in Pima County?

Deeds for Pima County land are recorded with the Pima County Recorder's Office in Tucson. Arizona law makes the county where the property sits the place to record. Under A.R.S. 33-411, an instrument affecting real property does not give notice to later buyers or lenders who paid value without notice unless it is recorded in the office of the county recorder of that county. For a seller, that means a signed deed is not the end of the job until it is on the public record.

The Recorder's site offers a public records search, an e-recording page, a document pickup page and a subscription for document services. The home page links to maps for 240 N Stone Avenue and 6920 E Broadway Boulevard in Tucson. Check the Recorder's contact page for current hours before you drive over.

The Recorder also runs elections and voter registration, so the same website carries a lot of voting information. Look for the Recording Fees, Recording Requirements and Recording FAQ links when you only need deed help.

What does Pima County charge to record a deed?

Recording an ordinary document costs a flat $30. That figure comes from A.R.S. 11-475, which sets $30 per instrument for papers required or authorized by law to be recorded, and $15 when a government body is a party and asks for the recording. The Recorder's schedule was last revised April 15, 2022.

The fee does not change with the sale price. The county schedule lists per-document charges only, and the statute notes that the $30 includes the amount charged under section 11-475.01. If you want to know whether any other charge applies to a particular deed, ask your title company or the Arizona Department of Revenue.

How can you pay the Pima County Recorder?

The office accepts Visa, Mastercard, cash, checks and money orders payable to Pima County Recorder. Credit cards are taken only for in-person transactions, not by phone or by mail. Online purchases carry a 2 percent card convenience fee.

Two rules trip up mailed packets, so read them before you send anything.

  • Checks must be pre-printed with your name.
  • Checks and money orders must be dated within 60 days of the Recorder receiving them.

Military discharge papers recorded under A.R.S. 11-465 carry no charge. Copies of recorded documents cost $0.25 per 8 1/2 by 11 inch image and $0.25 per digital document, while subdivision plats and survey maps are charged separately at $24 for the first image and $20 for each additional image.

What must a deed look like before the Recorder accepts it?

It needs a caption, original signatures, a legible original or copy, and a legal description, plus an affidavit of property value unless the transfer is exempt. The Recorder's Recording Requirements page and A.R.S. 11-480 set out the physical rules, and a document that fails them may be rejected at the counter.

  • Each instrument needs a caption briefly stating what it is, such as warranty deed.
  • Pages may be no larger than 8 1/2 inches by 14 inches, in type no smaller than ten point.
  • Margins must be at least one-half inch, and the first page needs a two inch blank top margin reserved for recording information.
  • A document that modifies an earlier one must state the earlier recording date and its docket and page or sequence number.

Arizona also requires that a deed be signed by the grantor and acknowledged before an authorized officer (A.R.S. 33-401). The Pima Recorder says it has been told by the County Attorney's Office not to give legal advice, so questions about which deed to use belong with an attorney or title company.

Do you need photo ID to record in person in Pima County?

Yes, starting September 8, 2026. The Recorder's office now requires valid photo identification from customers who present documents for recording in person, under A.R.S. 11-472. Accepted forms include a state driver's license, a state identification card, a tribal enrollment card or other tribal identification, and identification issued by a federal, state or local government.

The statute exempts documents submitted by an escrow officer, a title insurer or agent, a state or federally chartered bank or credit union, an active member of the State Bar of Arizona, or a governmental entity. Most sellers who close through escrow never see this step, because the escrow office handles the recording. The recorder may note the type, name and number of the ID but may not keep a copy, and that note is not a public record.

What is the affidavit of property value, and who is exempt?

It is a form signed by buyer and seller that must be attached to a deed at recording, and the Recorder must refuse a deed that lacks a complete one unless it carries an exemption notation (A.R.S. 11-1133). The statute asks for the buyer and seller names, the legal description, the sale date, the total consideration and whether the home will be owner-occupied or rented. The Arizona Department of Revenue supplies the form.

Some transfers are exempt under A.R.S. 11-1134. Examples in the statute:

  • A deed of gift.
  • A quitclaim deed made for no monetary consideration.
  • A trustee's deed under a deed of trust, and a transfer solely to provide or release security for a debt.
  • A transfer of residential property for only nominal consideration between spouses, parent and child, grandparent and grandchild, or siblings.
  • A transfer under a beneficiary deed with only nominal consideration.

Pima's Recording Requirements page says transfers claiming an exemption must be accompanied by the Department of Revenue exemption letter and number at recording. Check the exact notation with your title company before you submit.

What is Pima County like for sellers?

Pima County covers 9,189 square miles in south central Arizona, and Tucson is both its seat and its largest city. It was created in 1864 from land acquired in the Gadsden Purchase, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 1,074,685 residents. Beyond Tucson, the incorporated places include South Tucson, Marana, Oro Valley and Sahuarita, and large unincorporated communities such as Casas Adobes and Catalina Foothills.

Census figures for 2020 to 2024 show 65.2 percent of housing units owner-occupied, a median owner-occupied home value of $319,700, median gross rent of $1,212 and median household income of $70,315. The county holds 437,827 households. For a seller, the recording steps above are the same wherever the house sits in the county, but property tax is billed by the Pima County Treasurer at 240 N. Stone Avenue, so request a tax figure from that office before closing.

Does Pima County charge a transfer tax on a home sale?

The Recorder's fee schedule lists no charge based on the sale price. You pay the flat recording fee and complete an affidavit of property value. For any other charge on a specific deed, ask your title company or the Arizona Department of Revenue.

Can the Pima County Recorder help me fill out a deed?

No. The Pima County Recorder's Office is under instruction from the County Attorney's Office not to give legal advice or guidance. Use an attorney, escrow officer or title company to prepare the deed, then the Recorder checks it against the form rules.

What happens if I never record the deed?

Under A.R.S. 33-411, an unrecorded instrument gives no notice to later buyers or encumbrance holders who paid value without notice. That leaves the new owner exposed, so the deed should be recorded promptly after closing.

Where do you record a deed in Pinal County?

It says the new fee already covers the affidavit of property value, additional indexing and the document and storage fee surcharge, and each recording fee includes $1 for postage to return the document by mail.

  • Subdivision plats or maps (24 by 36 inches): $24, with $20 for each additional sheet.
  • Survey and other maps (18 by 24 inches): $24, with $20 for each additional sheet.
  • Plats and survey maps recorded at a government agency's request: $14 for the first sheet and $10 for each additional sheet.
  • Copies of recorded documents: $1 per page, with mail requests including return postage, plus $3 per document for certification.

The schedule shows flat per-document amounts and no charge that varies with the price of the house. If you want to confirm that nothing else applies to your sale, ask the title company handling the closing.

How do you submit a document to the Pinal County Recorder?

You can record in person at any of the five offices, by mail, or electronically through a Pinal County trusted e-recording partner. For mail, send the original document with a check or money order for the amount on the fee schedule. For e-recording, contact an office for the list of partners. The county's online document search covers records from May 23, 1980 to the current end date, and downloaded images carry an unofficial copy watermark.

Photo ID is required for in-person recording under A.R.S. 11-472, with exceptions for documents submitted by an escrow office, a title insurer or agent, a bank or credit union, an active State Bar of Arizona member, or a government entity. Most sellers who close through escrow skip this because the escrow office submits the deed.

The Recorder describes what happens after you submit a compliant document in order.

  • If the form is complete and the fees are paid, the office makes it a permanent public record.
  • Data entry creates an index so the record can be found by name.
  • The document is optically scanned and microfilmed to meet state archival requirements.
  • The original returns to the address typed on it.

Form rules appear in A.R.S. 11-480: a caption, an original, original signatures, a page no larger than 8 1/2 by 14 inches in type of ten point or larger, and a two inch top margin on page one.

Does Pinal County have a transfer tax, and what is the affidavit of property value?

County assessors and the Department of Revenue use the data to build tables for uniform valuation. The county adds that data from one sale does not directly change the assessment or taxes on that property.

The affidavit is signed, notarized and submitted to the Recorder. Exempt transfers skip it. Under A.R.S. 11-1134, a deed of gift, a quitclaim deed for no monetary consideration, a trustee's deed, a transfer between spouses, parent and child, grandparent and grandchild or siblings for only nominal consideration, and a transfer under a beneficiary deed with only nominal consideration are all on the list.

If your transfer is exempt, the county instructs you to write the statute number and exemption code on the face of the deed beneath the legal description. Its example is "A.R.S. 11-1134 B3." Do not complete the affidavit in that case.

What if you need to fix or remove something on a recorded record?

The only way to change the public record is another recording. The county explains that once an instrument of transfer has been recorded, a later recorded document is how ownership changes. Two other points from the county's FAQ are useful to a seller.

  • To see easements on your property, check Schedule B of your title policy if the purchase closed through a title company. Otherwise search the Recorder's website using one party's name and an approximate recording date.
  • People who want personal information removed from public records should read the separate Arizona statutes for the Recorder (A.R.S. 11-483), the Assessor and Treasurer (A.R.S. 11-484) and voter registration (A.R.S. 16-153).

The office also warns that it may refer suspicious documents to the FBI or other law enforcement, and that presenting a false instrument for recording is a class 6 felony under A.R.S. 39-161.

Yes. You can mail the original with a check or money order, or record electronically through a trusted e-recording partner. Contact a Pinal County Recorder's office for the partner list. Mail requests need the amount from the current fee schedule.

What does the Coconino County Recorder do when a house sells?

The County Recorder takes in the deed that moves title to a buyer and puts it on the public record, along with the mortgage releases and liens that affect the house. In Coconino County those records belong to the Flagstaff office, and the county's online records portal lists Treasurer, Assessor, GIS and Recorder links side by side.

Most sellers never visit the counter. A title or escrow company prepares the deed, gathers signatures, pays the fee and records it. Still, a seller who knows what the office requires can catch errors, particularly on inherited or family transfers where paperwork is handled by hand.

What does Arizona law say a recorder may charge?

Arizona sets recorder fees in A.R.S. 11-475, and the base charge for most documents is $30 per instrument. The figures below come straight from that statute.

ServiceFee
Papers required or authorized by law to be recorded, unless the fee is set elsewhere$30 per instrument

The $30 and $15 charges already include an amount collected under another section, 11-475.01. Copies for a state agency's official use cost half the usual fee, and the recorder collects nothing from the county office where the document is to be recorded when public money would pay the fee. The recorder also charges no fee to record or release a restitution lien or a lien to enforce a support order.

Read the full fee statute if you need an official figure, since the Coconino County Recorder's counter may post a current schedule.

What is an affidavit of legal value, and who signs it?

Most deeds that transfer title, and contracts for the sale of real property, must carry an affidavit of legal value signed by buyer and seller, or by an agent of either (A.R.S. 11-1133). It uses a form approved by the Arizona Department of Revenue. The recorder must refuse to record a deed without a complete affidavit unless the instrument notes a statutory exemption.

The affidavit collects the facts about the sale:

  • Names, mailing addresses and phone numbers of buyer and seller.
  • The address where a tax statement should go.
  • The legal description, the street address and the date of sale.
  • The total price, any cash down payment and the type of financing: cash, a new third-party loan, a seller loan, an assumption, or an exchange.
  • Whether personal property worth five percent or more of the price changed hands.
  • The assessor's parcel number.
  • The conditions of the sale, including any relationship between the parties.
  • How the property is used and, for a house, whether it will be owner-occupied or rented.

An affidavit counts as complete when each item is answered or marked not applicable. Leaving a line blank is a common reason for a rejected recording.

Does a house sale in Coconino County pay a transfer tax?

We did not find a transfer tax in the recorder fee statute or the affidavit statute, so we cannot say one applies. The exemption statute does mention "the affidavit and fee required by this article," which means the affidavit itself carries a fee. Ask the County Recorder or the Arizona Department of Revenue for the current amount.

Instead of guessing, ask your escrow officer to itemize every recording charge on the settlement statement. The Coconino County recording line should show the $30 base fee per instrument, or a higher total if several documents are recorded together, such as a deed and a release of a prior lien.

What format rules can get a Coconino County document rejected?

A.R.S. 11-480 lets a recorder reject only an instrument that fails a short list of formal tests at the counter. A caption describing the instrument is required, such as warranty deed. It must be an original with original signatures, legible enough to copy, and no larger than 8.5 by 14 inches with type no smaller than ten point.

The first page needs a two inch top margin reserved for recording information, and the other margins need to be at least half an inch. If the first page does not meet the top margin rule, the person recording attaches a separate cover sheet with the title of the document. A document that changes an earlier recorded paper must cite the earlier recording date and its docket and page.

Once a recorder accepts an instrument, a later claim that it breached these rules cannot invalidate it.

What do you need to know about Coconino County before listing a house?

Coconino County covers 18,661 square miles, with Flagstaff as county seat and largest city, and a 2020 census count of 145,101 people. Of the county's 69,108 housing units, 25.7 percent were vacant and 59.2 percent of the occupied units were owned by their occupants.

A few Coconino County facts that can shape a sale:

  • The county was formed in 1891, with Flagstaff as its seat.
  • Interstate 40 and Interstate 17 meet at Flagstaff, and Amtrak and commercial flights serve the city.
  • Northern Arizona University is the biggest employer on a 2017 list, with 3,500 workers, ahead of W. L. Gore and Associates and Flagstaff Medical Center.
  • Reservation land covers 7,142 square miles of the county, so ask your title company about any parcel near it.

Within the county, a sale of a Flagstaff bungalow, a Page rental or a Williams cabin follows the same state recording steps. The Recorder at 110 East Cherry Avenue handles the filing, and the title company usually does the rest.

Where do you get a tax balance before recording a Coconino County deed?

The Coconino County Treasurer is at 110 E. Cherry Avenue in Flagstaff, with hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday. You can reach the office at (928) 679-8188, toll free at (877) 500-1818, or at treasurer@coconino.az.gov.

Tax is a lien from January 1 of the tax year, so the balance should be known before the deed is recorded. Escrow normally pays the Treasurer from the seller's proceeds at closing, and then the deed is submitted to the Recorder.

Who records documents on behalf of an out-of-town seller?

Most recordings are submitted by the escrow or title company, which also pays the fee. If you plan to handle a family or estate transfer yourself, call the Recorder first and ask which forms the office wants. Statute requires original signatures on a recorded instrument, so a photocopy of a signed deed will not do.

Arizona's fee statute sets $30 per instrument for most recorded papers, and the county page for Coconino lists the same flat fee for basic recordings. Government parties pay $15 per instrument when they ask for the recording.

What is an affidavit of legal value in Arizona?

It is a form signed by buyer and seller, or their agents, that gives the price, financing type, parcel number and other facts about a sale. The recorder must reject a deed without it unless the deed cites an exemption.

Does a gift deed need the affidavit in Arizona?

No. A deed of gift is on the exemption list in A.R.S. 11-1134, and the instrument has to state the exemption on its face. Check with the Recorder or a title company before relying on it.

What size and margins must a recorded document have?

A recorded instrument can be no larger than 8.5 by 14 inches, with type of at least ten point, a two inch top margin on page one and half inch margins elsewhere. A cover sheet can fix a first page that falls short.

Where do you record a deed in Yuma County?

What are your options for recording a document in Yuma County?

The county lists three routes: in person, by mail and electronically. Which one you use depends mostly on who is closing the sale. Title and escrow companies normally record electronically, while individual owners often bring the paper deed to the counter.

What has to accompany a deed in Yuma County?

A deed that transfers title needs an affidavit, and A.R.S. 11-1133 spells out the rule. Buyer and seller, or an agent for either, certify the details on a Department of Revenue form, and the recorder has to refuse a deed that lacks a complete affidavit unless it is marked as exempt.

The affidavit asks for details that the Assessor later uses to update the parcel:

  • the buyer and seller names, addresses and phone numbers, and where to send the tax statement
  • the legal description, street address and assessor's parcel number
  • the sale date, the total consideration, the cash down payment and the type of financing

A.R.S. 11-1134 exempts transfers such as deeds of gift, court-ordered conveyances, no-money quitclaims, confirmation or correction deeds, transfers to create joint tenancy with right of survivorship, and trustee's deeds under a deed of trust. The instrument must name the exemption it claims. The Recorder's FAQ list includes both "What is an Affidavit of Real Property Value?" and "What is an Exemption Code?", so ask the office if the form confuses you.

What questions does the Yuma County Recorder answer?

The county's recorder FAQ lists 23 questions. Several matter to someone selling a house, and the office is the place to ask about any of them.

  • Whether the office offers notary service

The Assessor's FAQ adds that a copy of a deed comes from the Recorder, that the Assessor's online records show owners and sale prices, and that a manufactured home or recreational vehicle not affixed to real property is retitled at the Motor Vehicle Division, 2165 E. What taxes and liens affect a Yuma County sale?

Property tax rides along with the house until it is paid. A.R.S. 42-17153 makes the tax a lien that attaches on January 1 of the tax year and ranks ahead of other liens and encumbrances, except state liens and liens for taxes of other years. Your title company will order a payoff figure from the Treasurer before it records the deed.

The Treasurer's calendar shows 2026 first-half taxes were due October 1 and became delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 2, 2026, a date that has passed. The second half is due March 1, 2027 and delinquent after May 3, 2027. A 5 percent penalty applies on January 1, 2027 to delinquent 2025 taxes, and the lien sale for those years is February 18, 2027, with payment due by 5:00 p.m. on February 17 to avoid it.

Call the Treasurer at (928) 539-7781 for a balance. If you want to confirm how the county classified your home, the Assessor's Notice of Value explains the code for owner-occupied residences and rentals.

What should a seller know about Yuma County itself?

Yuma County fills the southwestern corner of Arizona, with an area of 5,519 square miles. It borders California across the Colorado River and the Mexican state of Sonora to the south, and the lowest point in Arizona is on the river at San Luis. The 2020 census counted 203,881 people, and the county seat is the city of Yuma.

The county's own pages list the incorporated places as the City of Yuma, the City of San Luis, the City of Somerton and the Town of Wellton, plus the community of Dateland. The county was one of four original Arizona counties, created by the first territorial legislature, and lost its northern half when La Paz County was formed in 1982.

Yuma County government publishes recorder forms and a recorded-documents search through the Recorder's menu. Owner names, parcel numbers and sale data are on the Assessor's online records site at yumacountyaz-assessor.tylerhost.net/assessor/web, which is the quickest way to confirm a parcel number before you fill out the affidavit.

Where is the Yuma County Recorder's office?

The office is at 298 S. Main Street, Yuma, AZ 85364, and the county calls it a new address. Hours are 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on weekdays, and the phone number is (928) 373-6020. Mailed documents go to Attention: Recording Division at the same address.

Can I record a deed electronically in Yuma County?

Yes, through third-party providers. The county names Data Services, Inc., eRecording Partners Network, Indecomm Global Services, CSC eRecording and Simplifile. Contact one of them directly, since the Recorder's page lists them as the e-recording options rather than a county portal.

Ask the Recorder's Office at (928) 373-6020 for the current amount before you mail anything. For mailed documents, the county asks for a check or money order payable to Yuma County Recorder. Your title company will include the recording charge on the closing statement.

Does a Yuma County deed need an affidavit of property value?

Usually yes. A.R.S. 11-1133 requires an affidavit of legal value with each deed that transfers title, and the recorder must refuse an incomplete one. A.R.S. 11-1134 lists exempt transfers, and the deed must state the exemption claimed.

How do I get a copy of my Yuma County deed?

Request it from the Yuma County Recorder's Office. The Assessor's FAQ directs deed copy requests to the Recorder, and the Recorder's FAQ has an entry on how to obtain a copy of your deed. Call (928) 373-6020 to ask about the request process and any copy charge.

The office does two jobs: it processes documents tied to real estate transactions, and it keeps voter registration records for the county. Sellers deal with the first job.

What sort of county is Cochise County?

Cochise County covers 6,219 square miles in the southeastern corner of Arizona and borders Mexico on its south side. Wikipedia lists it as close in size to Rhode Island and Connecticut combined, with a 2020 population of 125,447.

The county was founded February 1, 1881. Bisbee is the county seat, and the courthouse there is an art deco building. Sierra Vista is the largest city. The county neighbors Santa Cruz, Pima, Graham and Greenlee counties in Arizona and Hidalgo County in New Mexico.

Protected land is a big part of the map. What does it cost to record a deed in Cochise County?

What is the affidavit of real property value, and who needs it?

Every property sale needs a completed affidavit of real property value or an exemption number, and the Recorder will refuse the deed without one. The county's FAQ says all sale transactions require it, and it points questions to the Arizona Department of Revenue at 602-716-6843.

The statute behind it is A.R.S. 11-1133. Seller and buyer jointly certify details such as names and mailing addresses, a tax statement address, the legal description, the date of sale, total consideration and financing type, the assessor's parcel number, and whether the home will be owner-occupied or rented. Section 11-1134 lists the exemptions, and the instrument has to carry a note of the exemption claimed.

Examples of exempt transfers include a deed of gift, a deed made under court order, and a nominal-consideration transfer between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, or siblings. A sale for delinquent taxes is also listed.

What happens to a deed after it reaches the Recorder?

If the document meets form requirements, is complete and carries the right fee, the office accepts it and makes it permanent public record. The county describes the steps in its FAQ:

  1. The data entry department keys the key details to build an index.
  2. The microfilm department films and optically scans the document.
  3. The original is returned to the address typed on the document.
  4. A certified copy can be ordered later if the original is lost.

The county says to allow 15 to 20 business days for documents to come back. That is worth knowing if you are mailing a deed and want the original in hand. Your title or escrow company often handles the recording for a sale, so ask them before you plan a trip.

Who do I contact for a recording question?

Call 520-432-8350 or the toll free line at 888-457-4513 during office hours, or email through the link on the Recorder page. The county says forms for recording are available at most office supply or stationery stores, so the office does not hand them out.

For a homestead question, the FAQ points to A.R.S. 33-1101 and an attorney. For a business name, it points to A.R.S. 44-1236 and the Arizona statutes on entities. The Recorder describes what it records, but it does not offer legal advice on how to title your house.

Can the Recorder tell me about liens, owners and foreclosures?

Partly. Records at the office are found by searching a grantor and grantee name index, and you can run your own title search in person or hire a title company. The county's FAQ says it cannot tell you the owner by parcel number, which is a job for the Assessor at 520-432-8650.

  • To see liens on a property, search the index in the office or ask a title company.
  • To learn a selling price, come in and look for a recorded affidavit of real property value.
  • To research a foreclosure, get the owner's name or street address and visit the office.
  • For adding or removing a name, using a trust or removing a decedent from a deed, the county points people to a title company or an attorney.

How does recording tie into selling an inherited or tax-delinquent Cochise house?

Recording is the last public step in a sale, and several documents may reach this office along the way. A beneficiary deed must be recorded before the owner's death to work under A.R.S. 33-405. An affidavit of succession for a small estate is recorded here after the court registrar issues a certified copy (A.R.S. 14-3971). A certificate of redemption after a tax lien sale may be recorded here too (A.R.S. 42-18154).

If your Cochise County house has one of those issues, gather the recorded paperwork first. A title company can then tell you what must be cleared before a deed to a buyer can be recorded.

The county says to expect 15 to 20 business days. The original returns to the address typed on the document.

The county FAQ says to consult a title company or an attorney. The same answer applies to moving property into or out of a trust and to removing a decedent's name from a deed.

Yes, unless an exemption applies. The Recorder requires a completed affidavit or an exemption number on every sale, and the Arizona Department of Revenue can answer form questions.

No. The county refers owner-by-parcel questions to the Assessor at 520-432-8650. The Recorder searches by grantor and grantee name.

What are the rules for recording a document in La Paz County?

The document must be on paper and meet the layout rules the county publishes on its Document Recording Information page. A document that fails the state requirements is returned unrecorded, and so is a document sent without the correct fees. The Recorder's Office cannot help you prepare a document.

Does a La Paz County deed need an Affidavit of Property Value?

Yes, unless the deed is exempt. A.R.S. 11-1133 requires a deed that evidences a transfer of title to carry an affidavit completed by the buyer and the seller, or their agents, on a form the Arizona Department of Revenue approves. The recorder must refuse to record a deed that lacks a complete affidavit and has no exemption notation.

The La Paz County Forms page offers the Affidavit of Property Value, a list of exempt codes, the fee schedule PDF and a recording cover sheet. The county's FAQ says every property sale needs a completed affidavit or an exemption number, and it refers questions to the Arizona Department of Revenue at 602-716-6843.

  • Exempt transfers under A.R.S. 11-1134 include a deed of gift, a quitclaim deed given for no money, a conveyance under a court order, and a deed that confirms or corrects an earlier recorded deed.
  • Transfers for nominal consideration between spouses, between parents and children, between grandparents and grandchildren, and between siblings also qualify.
  • A trustee's deed under a power of sale, a transfer into or out of a trust for nominal consideration, and a transfer to create joint tenancy with right of survivorship are on the list as well.
  • An exempt deed must note the specific exemption on its face at the time of recording.

How much does the La Paz County Recorder charge?

Arizona law sets the base fee at $30 per recorded instrument, or $15 when a government body is a party and asks for the recording. A.R.S. 11-475 says those amounts include the charge under section 11-475.01.

Copies cost $1 for each page, according to the county's FAQ, and statute adds $3 for the recorder's certificate and seal on a certified copy. If you mail a request, the county asks for a self-addressed stamped envelope and the instrument number. The county's FAQ sends fee questions to the posted fee schedule or to the office at 928-669-6136.

A package that arrives short is returned unrecorded. Ask your title company to confirm the exact amount with the Recorder before the deed goes out, and keep the amount on the settlement statement.

Is there a transfer tax when you record a deed in La Paz County?

Article 9, Section 24 of the Arizona Constitution bars the state, counties, cities and districts from imposing any new tax, fee, stamp requirement or other assessment on the act of selling or transferring real property. Charges that already existed on December 31, 2007 are not covered by that rule.

For a seller, the practical question is which charges appear on the closing statement. The recording fee is one of them. The affidavit is a reporting form that the county assessor and the Department of Revenue use to track sales. Ask the title company to itemize everything tied to recording so you can compare it against the county fee schedule.

How can you find a recorded document in La Paz County?

Search the document images online, or ask a title company to run a search. The county's FAQ gives specific routes for common needs:

  • To find a sale price, search the document images and choose the document type affidavit of property value.
  • To find prior owners, search the grantor and grantee name index, or ask a title company for a title search.
  • To find an owner's name for a parcel, call the County Assessor at 928-669-6165.
  • To see a subdivision plat, request it from the Recorder in person or by mail, and have the map book and page number from the deed ready.

A certified or plain copy of a recorded document can be requested by instrument number, in person or by mail.

Do you need an Affidavit of Property Value to record a deed in Graham County?
